steps.description: Analyze the vulnerability and locate the Jackson deserialization entry point in the source code

suggestions: Search for Jackson's readValue() calls — that is where deserialization happens and where the attack surface is.
Also look for @JsonTypeInfo annotations and ObjectMapper configurations.

steps.description: Understand the empty key attack vector and why post-deserialization validation is insufficient

suggestions: The empty key ('') attack exploits special handling during Jackson parsing — it cannot be detected by examining the deserialized object.
The fix must be applied BEFORE readValue() is called — pre-deserialization validation on the raw JSON string.
warnings: Post-deserialization validation (validating the resulting Java object) is INSUFFICIENT — the attack has already executed by the time your code examines the object.

steps.description: Implement pre-deserialization validation to detect and reject malicious JSON patterns before readValue()

failure_patterns.reason: ⚠️ Validating the deserialized Java object AFTER readValue() cannot detect empty-key attacks — the attack already executed during deserialization. Implement validation on the RAW JSON string BEFORE readValue().

suggestions: Intercept the raw JSON string at the sampler entry point and check for empty keys before passing to readValue().
A simple approach: if rawJson.contains('"":') or rawJson.matches(.*""\s*:.*) → throw an exception.

steps.description: Create patch files (.patch) for the affected source files
Apply patches and rebuild with Maven — verify compilation succeeds

suggestions: Run 'mvn clean compile' to verify the patched code compiles without errors before testing.

steps.description: Verify fix blocks the empty-key exploit while preserving legitimate deserialization functionality
